Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JERUSALEM (CNN)  -- The international group Human Rights Watch is accusing Israel of firing weapons containing white phosphorus into Gaza. The group demands that the alleged practice cease. Israel is declining to say whether bursts like this over Gaza involve white phosphorus. The group's  researchers in Israel "observed multiple air-bursts of artillery-fired white phosphorus over what appeared to be the Gaza City/Jabaliya area" on Friday and Saturday, the organization said on its Web site. "Israel appeared to be using white phosphorus as an 'obscurant' [a chemical used to hide military operations], a permissible use in principle" under the laws of war, the HRW posting said. "However, white phosphorus has a significant, incidental, incendiary effect that can severely burn people and set structures, fields, and other civilian objects in the vicinity on fire," the posting said. "The potential for harm to civilians is magnified by Gaza's high population density, among the highest in the world." HRW said the use of white phosphorus in Gaza would violate "the requirement under international humanitarian law to take all feasible precautions to avoid civilian injury and loss of life." Last week, an Israel Defense Forces spokesman told CNN: "I can tell you with certainty that white phosphorus is absolutely not being used." Now, however, Israeli officials have a different response to questions about the possible use of phosphorus: "Any munitions that Israel is using are in accordance with international law. Israel does not specify the types of munitions or the types of operations it is conducting." Still, a doctor familiar with the material said it is not possible to tell, based on pictures of burns, whether white phosphorus was responsible. "Dead tissue pretty much looks the same," said Dr. Peter Grossman, president of the Grossman Burn Center in Sherman Oaks, California. The chemical "can burn down houses and cause horrific burns when it touches the skin," said Marc Garlasco, senior military analyst at Human Rights Watch. Since January 3, when Israel began its ground offensive in Gaza, news reports have circulated about the possible use of white phosphorus by the IDF. HRW's assertion was supported by munitions experts and some Palestinian doctors, including Nafiz Abu Sha'aban, who said the burns it caused were unlike anything he has seen in 27 years of practice. Watch footage of burn patients in Gaza . Though most severely burned patients have been sent to Egypt, the ongoing fighting has made it impossible to evacuate all of them, including one man with deep burns over 47 percent of his body, the doctor said. White phosphorus is known to burn flesh down to the bone. It's intended to provide illumination or to create a smokescreen in battle. Under an international protocol ratified by Israel in 1995, the use of such incendiary weapons is allowed when "not specifically designed to cause burn injury to persons." There is no prohibition per se against white phosphorus in conflict. But the timing and location of its use are restricted. For example, it is illegal under the protocol to use white phosphorus against any personnel, civilian or military. It can be directed only against military targets. International law says incendiary weapons cannot be used where civilians are concentrated. A house north of Gaza City was hit Sunday by something that observers contend may have been white phosphorus. "It's been burning since one o'clock in the morning," Munir Hammada told CNN 11 hours later. "If you move it with your feet, it reignites. You can't put it out with water, only sand." Those characteristics match the properties of white phosphorus, which ignites on contact with air.

In a statement published on its website, HRW said its Israel-based researchers witnessed several airbursts on Friday and Saturday that appeared to come from artillery shells containing white phosphorus over the Gaza City and Jabaliya area.

The organization said Israel seemed to be employing the substance as an obscurant—a chemical used to conceal military activity—which is generally permitted under the laws of armed conflict. However, HRW warned that white phosphorus also has powerful incendiary properties and can inflict severe burns and ignite nearby buildings, farmland, and other civilian property. According to the group, the danger is especially serious because Gaza has one of the world’s highest population densities.

HRW argued that using white phosphorus in Gaza would breach the international humanitarian-law obligation to take every feasible precaution to prevent civilian deaths and injuries.

An Israel Defense Forces representative told CNN the previous week that he could state definitively that white phosphorus was not in use. Israeli officials later changed their response, saying only that every weapon Israel employs complies with international law and that the country does not disclose details about its munitions or military operations.

Dr. Peter Grossman, president of the Grossman Burn Center in Sherman Oaks, California, cautioned that photographs of burn injuries alone cannot establish whether white phosphorus caused them, because dead tissue generally has a similar appearance regardless of the cause.

Marc Garlasco, then a senior military analyst with Human Rights Watch, said the substance can destroy homes by fire and produce devastating burns when it comes into contact with skin.

Reports suggesting that the IDF might be using white phosphorus had circulated since January 3, when Israel launched its ground operation in Gaza. HRW’s claim was backed by weapons specialists and several Palestinian physicians. Among them was Nafiz Abu Sha’aban, who said the resulting wounds differed from anything he had encountered during 27 years as a doctor. CNN also presented footage showing burn victims in Gaza.

According to Abu Sha’aban, most patients with the gravest burns had been transferred to Egypt. Continued combat, however, prevented everyone from being evacuated, including a man suffering deep burns across 47 percent of his body.

White phosphorus can burn human tissue all the way to the bone. In warfare, it is designed to light an area or produce a smoke screen.

Israel ratified an international protocol in 1995 under which incendiary weapons may be used if they are not specifically intended to burn people. White phosphorus is therefore not categorically banned in armed conflict, although international rules limit when and where it may be employed.

Under the protocol, white phosphorus cannot legally be used against people, whether civilians or members of the military, and may be aimed only at military objectives. International law also prohibits the use of incendiary weapons in places where civilians are concentrated.

On Sunday, a home north of Gaza City was struck by an object that observers believed could have contained white phosphorus. Eleven hours later, Munir Hammada told CNN that it had been burning since 1 a.m. He said moving the material with a foot caused it to ignite again and that water could not extinguish it; only sand was effective.

counterfactuals.output:
**Human Rights Watch accuses Israel of using white phosphorus in densely populated Gaza**

**JERUSALEM/GAZA —** Human Rights Watch has accused Israel of using white phosphorus over densely populated areas of Gaza, warning that the substance can cause severe burns and pose an indiscriminate risk to civilians when deployed in urban neighborhoods.

The rights group said it analyzed verified videos showing multiple airbursts of artillery-fired white phosphorus over Gaza City’s port on October 11, 2023. It also documented its use near the Israel-Lebanon border. Human Rights Watch said interviews with witnesses and an examination of the footage supported its findings.

White phosphorus ignites when exposed to oxygen, producing intense heat and thick white smoke. Militaries can lawfully use it to create smoke screens, illuminate targets or mark positions. But burning fragments can fall over a wide area, setting structures on fire and causing injuries that may penetrate to the bone and reignite if exposed to air.

Doctors working in Gaza have reported treating patients with unusually deep and persistent burns. Dr. Ahmed al-Mokhallalati, then a surgeon at Gaza City’s Al-Shifa Hospital, told reporters that some injuries were consistent with those caused by white phosphorus, though he said laboratory testing would be needed to establish the substance conclusively.

Israel has rejected allegations that it unlawfully used white phosphorus. The Israel Defense Forces has said its weapons are used in accordance with international law and that accusations of prohibited use are “unequivocally false.” Israel has previously said smoke-producing munitions in its arsenal are intended for concealment and not for targeting people.

White phosphorus itself is not universally prohibited under international law. However, its use is governed by the laws of armed conflict, including the requirements to distinguish between civilians and combatants, avoid disproportionate attacks and take all feasible precautions to limit civilian harm.

Protocol III of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons restricts the use of incendiary weapons in areas containing concentrations of civilians, particularly when delivered by air. Israel is not a party to that protocol, but remains bound by customary international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions’ protections for civilians.

Human Rights Watch said using airburst white phosphorus in crowded Gaza neighborhoods could violate the prohibition against indiscriminate attacks and called on Israel to stop using the substance in populated areas. It also urged stronger international restrictions covering all incendiary weapons, regardless of how they are delivered.

Independent access to Gaza has been heavily restricted, making it difficult for outside investigators to inspect impact sites, collect munition remnants or medically verify individual cases. Human Rights Watch’s allegations therefore rely primarily on visual evidence, witness accounts and weapons analysis, while Israel continues to dispute that its forces used white phosphorus unlawfully.

Researcher Marc Garlasco warned: “White phosphorus can burn down houses and cause horrific burns when it touches the skin. Israel should not use it in Gaza’s densely populated areas.” HRW’s Fred Abrahams later concluded: “The Israeli military didn’t just use white phosphorus in open areas as a screen for its troops. It fired white phosphorus repeatedly over densely populated areas,” despite the availability of less dangerous smoke shells.

Palestinian doctors described unusually severe injuries. Dr. Nafez Abu Shaaban of Gaza’s Shifa Hospital said: “We have never seen this type of injury or burn before,” reporting wounds that continued to smoke or reignite when exposed to air. Local residents likewise described burning material falling from the sky “like snow”; survivors interviewed by HRW spoke of “pieces of fire” entering homes and setting people, buildings, and fields alight.

Israeli officials initially rejected or narrowly framed the accusations. An army spokesperson said: “The IDF uses weapons in compliance with international law,” adding that weapons containing phosphorus were permitted for smoke-screening. Israel’s subsequent investigations acknowledged using white-phosphorus smoke projectiles but maintained that they were intended “for camouflage purposes” rather than as anti-personnel weapons. The military disciplined two senior officers over one incident involving shells fired toward a populated area, while denying a policy of deliberately targeting civilians.

White phosphorus is not categorically prohibited: militaries may use it for smoke or illumination. The controversy centered on its air-burst use over densely populated neighborhoods, hospitals, and a UN compound. HRW argued that such use was indiscriminate and therefore unlawful; Israel maintained that its purpose was lawful battlefield concealment and disputed claims that civilians had been intentionally attacked with it.

counterfactuals.output:
# Rights Groups Allege Israel Used White Phosphorus in Gaza’s Crowded Urban Areas

**January 19, 2009 — GAZA CITY**

Human-rights organizations and witnesses in the Gaza Strip are accusing Israeli forces of firing white-phosphorus munitions over densely populated parts of Gaza City and Jabaliya, raising urgent questions about whether the weapons were used in a way that violated international humanitarian law.

Amnesty International said Monday that its researchers in Gaza had found evidence of widespread phosphorus use, including still-burning wedges and artillery shells marked as containing white phosphorus. Human Rights Watch has also reported observing repeated airbursts from Israeli artillery that produced the distinctive pattern associated with the substance: a bright explosion followed by trails of burning material descending toward the ground.

The Israeli military has said it uses weapons permitted under international law and is investigating specific allegations. It has not provided a full public account of every munition fired during the offensive, which Israel launched on December 27 after years of rocket attacks by Palestinian armed groups and the collapse of a cease-fire.

The allegations come as residents, medical workers and United Nations personnel describe fires and burn injuries in and around some of Gaza’s most heavily populated districts. Israel announced a unilateral cease-fire over the weekend, while Hamas and other Palestinian factions subsequently declared their own truce, but humanitarian agencies are only beginning to assess the destruction.

## Claims in Gaza City and Jabaliya

Witnesses have described shells bursting in the air over Gaza City and the northern town and refugee-camp area of Jabaliya, scattering burning fragments that continued to emit thick white smoke.

Human Rights Watch said its researchers outside Gaza had observed what appeared to be white-phosphorus artillery rounds detonating above civilian areas. Amnesty International investigators who entered Gaza after the cease-fire said they found remnants they identified as components of American-made 155mm artillery shells designed to disperse white-phosphorus wedges.

One of the most serious incidents under scrutiny is the January 15 shelling of the main compound of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency in Gaza City. Hundreds of civilians had taken shelter there. UN officials said shells containing phosphorus struck the compound, setting fire to warehouses holding food, medicine and other emergency supplies.

UNRWA officials said they had repeatedly supplied the Israeli military with the coordinates of the facility. Israel said its forces had come under fire from the area and returned fire, an account disputed by UN officials.

Separate allegations concern attacks in and around Jabaliya, including areas near schools and residential neighborhoods. Rights groups say the apparent use of an area-effect munition there was especially dangerous because civilians in Gaza have had limited ability to flee the fighting. Israel had closed or tightly controlled the territory’s crossings, while combat was taking place in an exceptionally confined and crowded area.

The precise circumstances of each strike remain contested. Independent access to Gaza was severely restricted during much of the offensive, making immediate verification difficult.

## What white phosphorus does

White phosphorus is a chemical substance that ignites when exposed to oxygen. Military forces commonly use it to create smoke screens, mark targets or illuminate battlefields. It is not automatically prohibited under international law.

Once ignited, however, phosphorus burns at extremely high temperatures and can continue burning until it is deprived of oxygen or consumed. It can cause severe injuries if it lands on people or penetrates clothing. Particles embedded in a wound may reignite when exposed to air. The smoke can also be hazardous in enclosed or heavily contaminated areas.

Artillery shells carrying white phosphorus often burst in the air and scatter numerous burning pieces over a broad area. Rights organizations argue that this dispersal pattern makes the munition particularly hazardous when used over a city, refugee camp or other concentration of civilians.

Medical workers in Gaza have reported treating patients with unusual and deep burns, though determining the cause of individual injuries requires clinical and forensic examination. Not every white-burning explosion or severe burn proves phosphorus use, and rights groups say physical remnants, military records and witness testimony will be needed to establish responsibility for specific attacks.

## Why the legal issue depends on how it was used

The central legal question is not simply whether Israel possessed or fired white phosphorus. The issue is where, why and how the munitions were used.

International humanitarian law requires armed forces to distinguish between military targets and civilians. It prohibits indiscriminate attacks and attacks expected to cause civilian harm excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Commanders must also take feasible precautions to minimize civilian casualties.

White phosphorus may lawfully be used for purposes such as screening troop movements, provided its use complies with those rules. But rights groups contend that airbursting phosphorus shells over crowded neighborhoods can spread burning material too widely to distinguish adequately between fighters and civilians.

“If white phosphorus was fired directly over densely populated areas without taking all feasible precautions, its use could amount to an indiscriminate attack,” human-rights investigators have argued.

The legal analysis may also involve rules governing incendiary weapons. Protocol III to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons restricts attacks with air-delivered incendiary weapons against military objectives within concentrations of civilians and places limits on other incendiary attacks in such areas.

The application of that treaty is complicated. Israel is not bound by Protocol III in the same manner as states that have ratified it, and the protocol’s definition contains exceptions for munitions whose incendiary effect is incidental to another purpose, such as smoke or signaling. Even where the protocol does not directly apply, however, the broader customary rules of distinction, proportionality and precautions remain relevant.

Human-rights groups therefore say a claim that the shells were used to create smoke would not end the inquiry. Investigators would still have to determine whether less dangerous alternatives were available, whether civilians were present, whether adequate warnings were given and whether the expected military benefit justified the foreseeable risk.

## Possible war-crimes inquiry

A violation of the laws of war is not automatically a war crime. Criminal responsibility generally requires evidence that an unlawful attack was carried out intentionally or recklessly, with the necessary knowledge of civilian risks. Investigators would need to examine targeting decisions, orders, artillery logs, the location of Palestinian fighters and the precautions taken by Israeli forces.

Rights groups are calling for an independent investigation, arguing that military self-review alone will not be sufficient. They also say Palestinian armed groups must be investigated for launching rockets indiscriminately toward Israeli towns and for operating in ways that endangered Gaza’s civilian population.

Israel maintains that Hamas fights from residential areas, stores weapons near civilian buildings and uses the population as cover. Hamas denies deliberately using civilians as human shields. Even if Palestinian fighters unlawfully positioned themselves among civilians, humanitarian-law experts stress that Israel would remain obligated to distinguish targets, assess proportionality and take feasible precautions.

With Gaza’s streets only now becoming accessible to outside investigators, the full scale of phosphorus use—and whether particular attacks were lawful—remains unclear. Shell fragments, hospital records, photographs, witness accounts and Israeli operational documents are likely to determine whether the allegations can be substantiated.

For the civilians returning to burned homes and shelters in Gaza City and Jabaliya, the immediate concern is more practical: unexploded ordnance and phosphorus remnants may continue to pose a danger even after the fighting has stopped.

counterfactuals.output:
## Evidence and denials over white phosphorus in Gaza

**GAZA/JERUSALEM —** Human-rights groups and weapons specialists have cited video footage, photographs and witness accounts as evidence that Israeli forces fired white-phosphorus artillery rounds over Gaza, while the Israeli military has denied some allegations and said its weapons are used in accordance with international law.

Following the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, **Human Rights Watch said it verified videos recorded on Oct. 10 and 11 showing repeated airbursts over Gaza City’s port and nearby urban areas**. The organization said the distinctive pattern—artillery projectiles bursting overhead and scattering streams of burning material—was consistent with 155mm white-phosphorus rounds used to create smoke screens.

**Amnesty International’s Crisis Evidence Lab also reviewed imagery it said showed artillery units near Gaza equipped with U.S.-made M825 and M825A1 155mm rounds**, which contain white-phosphorus-impregnated felt wedges. Such markings establish the presence of the ammunition, though photographs of rounds near the battlefield do not by themselves prove where every shell was fired or how it was used.

Investigators also cited residents’ descriptions of dense smoke, burning particles and injuries compatible with exposure. White phosphorus ignites on contact with oxygen and can continue burning until deprived of it, causing deep thermal and chemical injuries. Independent verification inside Gaza has been limited by restricted access, continuing combat and the destruction of potential evidence.

The public evidence therefore supports allegations that white-phosphorus smoke rounds were present and apparently fired over Gaza, but it does not, in every reported incident, conclusively establish the intended target, the commander’s purpose or whether civilians were struck.

### Israel’s response

The Israel Defense Forces rejected allegations that it had unlawfully used white phosphorus. In responses to media inquiries and human-rights reports, the military said it used only lawful weapons and operated in compliance with international law. In some statements, it described particular claims of white-phosphorus use in Gaza as “unequivocally false” or said it was not aware of such use.

Israel has previously acknowledged employing white-phosphorus smoke munitions during the 2008-09 Gaza conflict, while maintaining they were used for screening rather than to attack civilians. After international criticism, the IDF said it had adopted restrictions and moved toward alternative smoke shells.

### What international law permits

White phosphorus is **not categorically banned**. It is generally not classified as a chemical weapon when used for illumination, signaling, marking targets or producing smoke, because its principal military effect is heat and combustion rather than toxicity.

Its use is nevertheless tightly constrained:

- It may be used to create smoke screens or conceal troop movements, provided the attack complies with the laws of war.
- Civilians and civilian objects may never be deliberately targeted.
- Forces must distinguish military targets from civilians, assess whether expected civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the anticipated military advantage, and take feasible precautions.
- Using white phosphorus in or near densely populated areas can be unlawful if its wide-area, uncontrollable burning effects make civilian harm foreseeable or disproportionate.

**Protocol III to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons** prohibits attacks on civilians with incendiary weapons and bans air-delivered incendiary attacks against military objectives located within concentrations of civilians. It also restricts ground-launched incendiaries in populated areas. The protocol excludes munitions designed primarily for smoke, signaling or illumination from its definition of an incendiary weapon, even if they have incidental incendiary effects—a provision that creates legal debate around white-phosphorus smoke shells.

Israel is not a party to Protocol III. It remains bound, however, by the broader customary rules of international humanitarian law, including distinction, proportionality and precautions in attack. Thus, the legality of any particular use depends not simply on the presence of white phosphorus, but on **where it was fired, why it was used, what precautions were taken and the foreseeable danger to civilians**.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

Human Rights Watch has alleged that Israeli forces used white phosphorus in Gaza, citing witness accounts and its review of photographs and videos showing airbursts of a substance that produced multiple streams of thick white smoke. The organization said using the incendiary material over populated areas could put civilians at grave risk.

Israel’s military has previously said its weapons comply with international law and has disputed allegations that it unlawfully used white phosphorus. CNN has not independently verified the substance responsible for the reported fires or burns.

Witnesses in Gaza described fiery fragments falling from the sky and igniting on contact. One resident said the material continued to burn even after people tried to smother it, while medical workers reported treating patients with deep burns that appeared to reignite when exposed to air.

Burn specialists urged caution, however. White phosphorus injuries can be difficult to distinguish from other thermal or chemical burns without laboratory testing, examination of debris or reliable documentation of the munition used. Severe burns, persistent smoke and reignition may be consistent with phosphorus exposure, experts said, but they are not definitive proof.

White phosphorus is a wax-like chemical that ignites when exposed to oxygen, producing intense heat and dense white smoke. Militaries may use it lawfully to create smoke screens, mark targets or illuminate terrain. It can also cause catastrophic injuries: particles may burn through skin and tissue, reignite when re-exposed to air and, if absorbed into the body, damage internal organs.

The substance is not prohibited in all circumstances under international law. But its use as an incendiary weapon against civilians, or in ways that fail to distinguish between civilians and military targets, can violate the laws of war. Human rights groups say deploying it in crowded urban areas creates an unacceptable risk because burning fragments can scatter over a wide area and start fires in homes, shelters and medical facilities.

Human Rights Watch called on the parties to preserve munition fragments, medical records and visual evidence so independent investigators can determine what was used. Experts said such an inquiry would require more than eyewitness accounts, including verified imagery, weapons analysis and environmental or tissue samples.
